frames.narration: Cohesion first: Pricing only prices and Inventory only tracks stock, so each changes for one reason. Now the question is how they depend on each other and on Checkout.
Version one shares one mutable state: every module reads and writes it. That is common coupling. Nothing calls anything, yet 14 dependencies exist through the state and the coupling score is 56.
A change request adds a currency field to the price structure. Checkout, Billing and Reports share that structure, so 3 other modules must change.

Version two has modules call each other directly, but they reach into each other's private fields and internal helpers instead of a public operation. That is content coupling, the tightest kind, and the score rises to 70.
Version three gives each module a narrow interface: Checkout passes plain values or one small object, and the Law of Demeter holds. The score falls to 10, with 6 dependencies.
The same new price field now reaches only Checkout, which passes the structure on. A rewrite of the stock logic reaches nobody else: its callers never saw the internals.

The trap: merge all 7 into one module to get zero dependencies. Now every change touches the one module and forces all 7 responsibilities to be re-tested. Coupling vanished from the graph, and cohesion went with it.
Aim for cohesive modules with narrow, explicit dependencies. Tight coupling inside one module owned by one team is cheap. Across a team boundary it is where changes get expensive.
